rewrites.summary:
For a trans traveler the material risk profile tracks the LGBTI-protection frame the record holds: same-sex intimacy was decriminalised in 2001 through an order imposed from the parent country after the local legislature refused, and in 2020 the Court of Appeal held that the marriage of a same-sex couple wed in another country must be recognised, which immigration authorities did for immigration effects — yet a statute effective 2022 confines family status to heterosexual marriage, and the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council rejected the challenge to it in March 2022. An unequal age of consent survived the 2001 reform.

Practical safety reads as tolerant and tourist-facing: in July 2021 roughly 600 people, including the premier, the governor and other ministers, joined the first Pride parade, one of the broadest official turnouts the community has seen, although organisers asked participants to refrain from excessive displays of affection amid public-space sensitivities.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Parent-authority policy turbulence frames the later recognition rulings: in 2009 legislators of the parent country criticised the draft constitution for deliberately excluding gay rights, calling the omission 'deplorable' and warning the drafting could leave local courts affording citizens less protection than the European Convention on Human Rights Article 14 requires, while the parent government countered that the discrimination-grounds list was open-ended.
rewrites.localsOnly: For residents, family status is the contested terrain: a statute confining family status to heterosexual marriage took effect in 2022, and equality advocates have operated mainly through immigration and recognition rulings rather than family law itself. The Grand Court's March 2019 strike-down of the same-sex marriage ban was overturned on appeal in August 2019, leaving only the recognition-for-immigration-effects line standing for the resident couples it protected.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: Territory of the United Kingdom; local deviations noted in summary. No source documents border-screening practice, documents handling, arrest patterns, or the operational enforcement of the unequal age of consent, and nothing on the record distinguishes protections or risks specific to trans travelers as opposed to same-sex couples. The practical working of the recognition-for-immigration-effects line at ports of entry is unverified.

blindSourceSummaries: A 2009 news report: national legislators on the parent nation's foreign-affairs committee criticised a draft constitution for deliberately excluding gay rights, calling the omission 'deplorable' and warning the drafting could leave local courts affording citizens less protection than the convention on human rights requires, while the parent nation's government countered that the discrimination-grounds list was open-ended — early evidence of friction between the parent nation and the state/province that frames the later recognition rulings.

A 2021 local news report: around 600 people — including the premier, the governor, ministers and other elected legislators — joined the local LGBTQ foundation's first Pride parade in July 2021, an historic turnout with broad official participation; participants were asked to refrain from excessive displays of affection amid public-space sensitivities — evidence of high official tolerance in the tourist-facing environment.

A 2020 news report: immigration authorities recognised the marriage of a same-sex couple wed in another country, the appeals court holding that refusing recognition would treat persons unequally on sexual-orientation grounds; a March 2019 first-instance strike-down of the marriage ban was later overturned on appeal in August 2019, but the recognition-for-immigration-effects line survived — the basis for the 'recognition without status' visitor posture.
rewrites.notes:
Split from the merged batch record per rule 6, derived only from current_summary and the three source claims: visitor risk (recognition-without-status posture, 2001 decriminalisation, 2022 statute + JCPC rejection, Pride safety signal) to summary (3 sentences, 2

); 2009 parent-parliament draft-constitution friction to tangentialFactors; resident family-status litigation terrain (2019 strike-down/overturn, advocacy through recognition rulings) to localsOnly; scope gaps (no border-screening/documents/arrest-relevant sources, trans-specific distinction unverifiable, ports-of-entry working unverified) to outOfScopeNotes. Blind mirrors are substitution-only per rule 7/7e: 'parent nation' for the administering country, 'national court' for the Privy Council, 'the court' for the Grand Court, 'state/province' for territory, 'convention on human rights' for the European Convention (Art 14 kept as a rater-weight fact only where visible and genericised in blind), names (Paul Pearson, Randall Pinder, Smellie, Cayman LGBTQ Foundation, FCO) dropped, 'historic' used only as the record's own adjective (not as the colonisation substitution).
